levels.title: Dev Environment
levels.tagline: Your tools shape your thinking. Set them up once, set them up right.
objectives: Set up Python 3.12+, Node.js 22+, and Rust toolchains from scratch
Configure virtual environments and package managers for reproducible builds
Verify GPU access with CUDA/MPS and run a test tensor operation
Understand the four-layer stack: system, packages, runtimes, AI libraries
levels.problem:
You're about to learn AI engineering across 200+ lessons using Python, TypeScript, Rust, and Julia. If your environment is broken, every single lesson becomes a fight against tooling instead of learning.

Most people skip environment setup. Then they spend hours debugging import errors, version conflicts, and missing CUDA drivers. We're going to do this once, properly.
levels.concept:
An AI engineering environment has four layers:

We install bottom-up. Each layer depends on the one below it.

code.code:
# macOS
xcode-select --install
brew install git curl wget

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential git curl wget

# Windows (use WSL2)
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

exercises: Run the verification script and fix any failures
Create a Python virtual environment for this course and install PyTorch
Write a "hello world" in all four languages and run each one

key_terms.reality: Your complete tool workspace: shell, editor, language runtimes, package managers, and GPU drivers — all configured to work together so you can write and run code without fighting tooling errors.
key_terms.myth: Just install Python and you're good.
key_terms.analogy: Like a chef's kitchen. You wouldn't cook in a kitchen with no knives, a broken stove, and missing ingredients. A dev environment is your prepared kitchen — everything in its place, tested and ready.
key_terms.example: You clone an AI repo. It runs first try because your environment has Python 3.13, CUDA 12.4, and the right PyTorch build already installed. Your friend clones the same repo but spends 2 hours debugging import errors because their environment was never set up properly.
key_terms.why_matters: Every lesson after this one assumes your environment works. If it's broken, every single line of code becomes a debugging session instead of a learning moment.
key_terms.common_trap: Skipping environment setup to 'save time' — then losing hours to version conflicts and cryptic import errors that a proper environment would have prevented.
key_terms.scenario: You clone an AI repo and run `python train.py`. You get 'ImportError: No module named torch'. What's the most likely root cause?
key_terms.when_to_use: Before writing any code in a new project, you need to ensure all tools and dependencies are installed and compatible.
key_terms.mini_challenge: Open your terminal. Run `python --version` and `node --version`. If either fails, you've found your first environment gap.

key_terms.reality: An isolated folder containing its own Python interpreter and packages. Projects can have different versions of the same library without conflict.
key_terms.myth: One global Python install works for everything.
key_terms.analogy: Each project gets its own toolbox. Your image-classifier project needs PyTorch 2.4. Your NLP project needs PyTorch 2.1. Two toolboxes, no fight.
key_terms.example: `uv venv` creates a .venv folder. Activate it and `pip install torch` only affects that project. Deactivate, and you're back to your clean system Python.
key_terms.why_matters: Without virtual environments, installing a package for one project can silently break another project. This is the #1 cause of 'it worked yesterday' bugs.
key_terms.common_trap: Installing packages globally with `pip install` without activating a venv first. Always check `which python` points to your .venv.
key_terms.scenario: Project A needs numpy 1.26. Project B needs numpy 2.0. You install both globally. What happens?
key_terms.mini_challenge: Create two venvs. Install numpy 1.26 in one and numpy 2.0 in the other. Verify they're isolated by running `python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'` in each.

key_terms.reality: A tool that downloads, installs, updates, and removes software packages — and crucially, resolves dependency trees so you don't have to manually track what depends on what.
key_terms.myth: Just download the .whl file and pip install it.
key_terms.analogy: Like an app store for code. You say 'I need PyTorch', it figures out which version, downloads it, installs all the things PyTorch needs, and tells you when updates are available.
key_terms.example: `uv pip install torch` — uv checks your Python version, your OS, your CUDA version, picks the right torch wheel, downloads it, and installs numpy as a dependency automatically.
key_terms.why_matters: Modern AI projects have 50-200+ dependencies. No human can track them manually. A good package manager is the difference between `pip install -r requirements.txt` in 10 seconds versus 2 hours of manual dependency hell.
key_terms.common_trap: Mixing package managers in the same environment (pip into conda, or uv and pip). Pick one per environment and stick with it.
key_terms.scenario: Your `pip install` command fails with 'Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement'. What should you check first?
key_terms.when_to_use: Every time you add a new library to your project, use your package manager instead of manually downloading files.

key_terms.reality: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform that lets you run code on thousands of GPU cores simultaneously. PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX all use CUDA under the hood for GPU acceleration.
key_terms.analogy: CUDA is like a highway system for your GPU. Without it, data trickles down a dirt road (CPU). With CUDA, data flows on an 8-lane highway — thousands of calculations happen at the same time instead of one after another.
key_terms.example: Training a CNN on CPU: 8 hours. Same training on GPU with CUDA: 10 minutes. The code is identical — PyTorch handles the CUDA part automatically via `model.to('cuda')`.
key_terms.why_matters: Without CUDA, deep learning is impractically slow. With CUDA, you can iterate on models in minutes instead of days. The speed difference is not 2x or 10x — it's often 50-100x for training.
key_terms.common_trap: Installing PyTorch without checking which CUDA version you have. `nvidia-smi` shows your CUDA version. Install the PyTorch build that matches.
key_terms.mini_challenge: Run `nvidia-smi` (or `system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType` on Mac). Find your GPU model and CUDA version. Then run `python -c 'import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())'`.

key_terms.reality: A command-line interface that lets you control your computer by typing commands instead of clicking. The shell runs programs, pipes data between them, and automates repetitive tasks.
key_terms.myth: Real developers use IDEs, not terminals.
key_terms.analogy: The shell is the cockpit of your computer. GUIs are like the passenger seat — you can see where you're going, but you can't fly the plane. The shell gives you direct control over every dial and switch.
key_terms.example: `find . -name '*.py' | xargs wc -l` — finds every Python file in your project and counts lines in one line. Doing this in a GUI file explorer would take 5+ minutes of clicking.
key_terms.why_matters: AI engineering involves running training scripts, managing files, checking GPU status, and deploying servers. Every one of these is a shell command. You don't need to be a shell wizard, but you need to be comfortable.
key_terms.common_trap: Being afraid of the terminal and trying to do everything through GUI tools. GUIs slow you down for repetitive tasks. Learn 10 shell commands and you'll be faster than any GUI.
key_terms.scenario: You need to find which Python files in your project use 'import torch'. Which one-liner does it?
key_terms.when_to_use: Whenever you need to run scripts, manage files in bulk, check system status, or automate anything repetitive.

labs.title: Assemble Your Environment
labs.prompt: You just got a new laptop. Arrange these steps in the right order to build a working AI dev environment.

steps.label: Install system packages (git, curl, build-essential)
Install Python 3.13 via uv: uv python install 3.13
Create a virtual environment: uv venv
Install PyTorch matching your CUDA version
Verify: python -c 'import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())'

labs.success: Environment ready! This is the foundation for every AI project you'll build.

labs.title: Spot the Broken Setup
labs.prompt: A teammate's environment isn't working. They ran these commands. Select all the MISTAKES:

blocks.label: pip install torch (no venv activated)
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
Installed PyTorch CPU-only but has an NVIDIA GPU
nvidia-smi (to check CUDA version)
sudo pip install (installing globally as root)

labs.success: Correct! Global installs, wrong CUDA builds, and forgetting venvs are the top 3 environment killers.

debugs.scenario: Your teammate ran `python train.py` and got 'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named torch'. They swear they installed it yesterday. What's broken?
options: They installed torch inside a venv but forgot to activate it today
Python is corrupted and needs reinstallation
The GPU driver crashed
They need to install CUDA from scratch
debugs.explain: The most common cause: torch was installed inside a venv, but they opened a new terminal and forgot to `source .venv/bin/activate`. Without activation, Python looks at system packages — where torch isn't installed. Fix: activate the venv and try again.
debugs.hint1: Think about where packages live. Is the torch they installed yesterday still visible today?
debugs.hint2: Check whether they're in the same environment. `which python` will tell you.

levels.title: Git & Collaboration
levels.tagline: Version control is not optional. Every experiment, every model, every lesson you build here gets tracked.
objectives: Configure git identity and use the daily workflow of add, commit, and push
Create and merge branches for isolated experiments without breaking main
Write a .gitignore that excludes model checkpoints and large binary files
Navigate the commit history with git log to understand project evolution
levels.problem:
You're about to write hundreds of code files across 20 phases. Without version control you will lose work, break things you can't undo, and have no way to collaborate with others.

Git is the tool. GitHub is where the code lives. This lesson covers what you need for this course and nothing more.
levels.concept:
Three things to remember:
1. Save often (`git commit`)
2. Push to remote (`git push`)
3. Branch for experiments (`git checkout -b experiment`)

code.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

exercises: Clone this repo, create a branch called my-progress, make a file, commit it, push it
Create a .gitignore that excludes model checkpoint files (.pt, .pth, .safetensors)
Look at the commit history of this repo with git log --oneline and read how lessons were added

key_terms.reality: A snapshot of your entire project at a point in time
A pointer to a commit that moves forward as you work
Taking changes from one branch and applying them to another
A copy of your repo hosted somewhere else (GitHub, GitLab)
A system that tracks every change to your code, lets you undo mistakes, experiment in branches without breaking the main code, and collaborate with others without stepping on each other's work.
key_terms.myth: Just save copies of files with different names — no need for Git.
key_terms.analogy: Like Google Docs version history, but for code. You can see who changed what, when, and why. You can rewind to any point in time. You can make a copy (branch), experiment freely, and merge back only the good parts.
key_terms.example: You're training a model and accidentally delete a critical data preprocessing function. Without Git: panic. With Git: `git checkout -- preprocess.py` — restored in 2 seconds from the last committed version.
key_terms.why_matters: Git is the universal language of software engineering. Every AI research lab, every company, every open-source project uses it. Not knowing Git is like being a writer who can't use a word processor.
key_terms.common_trap: Committing large model files (.pt, .pth, .bin) to Git. Git is for code, not model weights. Use .gitignore to exclude checkpoints and data files — they bloat the repo and slow everything down.
key_terms.scenario: You accidentally commit an API key to your public repo. What's the immediate remediation, and why does deleting the file and recommitting NOT fix the exposure?
key_terms.when_to_use: Every time you write code. Initialize a repo before you write the first line.

levels.title: GPU Setup & Cloud
levels.tagline: Training on CPU is fine for learning. Training for real needs a GPU.
objectives: Verify local GPU availability using nvidia-smi and PyTorch's CUDA API
Configure Google Colab with a T4 GPU for free cloud-based experiments
Benchmark matrix multiplication on CPU vs GPU and measure the speedup
Estimate the largest model that fits in your VRAM using the fp16 rule of thumb
levels.problem:
Most lessons in phases 1-3 run fine on CPU. But once you start training CNNs, transformers, or LLMs (phases 4+), you need GPU acceleration. A training run that takes 8 hours on CPU takes 10 minutes on GPU.

You have three options: local GPU, cloud GPU, or Google Colab (free).

code.code: nvidia-smi

exercises: Run the benchmark above and compare CPU vs GPU times
If you don't have a GPU, run it on Google Colab and compare
Check how much GPU memory you have and estimate the largest model you can fit (rule of thumb: 2 bytes per parameter for fp16)

key_terms.reality: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform that lets you run code on the GPU
Video RAM on the GPU, separate from system RAM. Limits model size.
16-bit floating point, uses half the memory of fp32 with minimal accuracy loss
Specialized GPU cores for matrix multiplication, 4-8x faster than regular cores

GPUs have thousands of cores designed for parallel math — exactly what neural networks need. Training on GPU is typically 50-100x faster than CPU. Without GPU access, deep learning is impractically slow.
key_terms.myth: Any computer with a graphics card can train LLMs.
key_terms.analogy: A CPU is a small team of geniuses (8-16 cores, each very fast at sequential work). A GPU is an army of clerks (thousands of cores, each simple but working simultaneously). For matrix multiplication — the core operation in deep learning — an army of clerks beats a small team of geniuses every time.
key_terms.example: Training ResNet-50 on ImageNet: CPU = 8 hours. NVIDIA A100 GPU = 10 minutes. Same code, 48x speedup. The only change is `model.to('cuda')`.
key_terms.why_matters: Without GPU acceleration, you can't iterate on models. What takes 10 minutes on GPU takes all day on CPU. You can't learn deep learning if every experiment takes 8 hours.
key_terms.common_trap: Buying the most expensive GPU without checking VRAM requirements. For inference, 8GB is often enough. For training 7B-parameter models, you need 24GB+. Match the GPU to your actual workload.
key_terms.scenario: You rent a cloud GPU but `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns False. The GPU is online and visible in the dashboard. What's most likely wrong?
key_terms.when_to_use: Any model training beyond trivial examples. Also for inference of models larger than ~1B parameters.
key_terms.mini_challenge: Run `nvidia-smi` (or check Google Colab's free GPU). How much VRAM is available? Could it fit a 7B parameter model in FP16 (14GB)?

levels.title: APIs & Keys
levels.tagline: Every AI API works the same way: send a request, get a response. The details change, the pattern doesn't.
objectives: Store API keys securely using environment variables and .env files
Make an LLM API call using both the Anthropic Python SDK and raw HTTP
Compare SDK-based and raw HTTP request/response formats for debugging
Identify and handle common API errors including authentication and rate limits
levels.problem: Starting from Phase 11, you'll call LLM APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google). In Phase 13-16 you'll build agents that use these APIs in loops. You need to know how API keys work, how to store them safely, and how to make your first API call.
levels.concept:
Every API call has:
1. An endpoint (URL)
2. An API key (authentication)
3. A request body (what you want)
4. A response body (what you get back)

code.code:
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

exercises: Get an Anthropic API key and make your first API call
Try the raw HTTP version and compare the response format to the SDK version
Intentionally use a wrong API key and read the error message

key_terms.reality: A secret string that authenticates you to a service (like OpenAI or Anthropic). It's like a password — anyone with your key can use the service as you and bill your account. Never commit API keys to Git.
key_terms.myth: Hardcoding the key in my script is fine — nobody else sees my code.
key_terms.analogy: Your house key. You wouldn't tape it to your front door. An API key in your public GitHub repo is the digital equivalent — anyone can find it with a 5-second search and use your account.
key_terms.example: BAD: `openai.api_key = 'sk-abc123...'` in committed code. GOOD: `openai.api_key = os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']` — key stays in a .env file that's in .gitignore.
key_terms.why_matters: Leaked API keys are the #1 security incident for AI developers. Attackers scan GitHub continuously for exposed keys. A leaked OpenAI key can rack up thousands of dollars in charges in hours.
key_terms.common_trap: Putting the key in a config file, then commenting it out before committing — the key is still in Git history! Once committed, you must revoke the key and rotate to a new one.
key_terms.scenario: You find your OpenAI API key on GitHub. What two actions must you take, and in what order?
key_terms.mini_challenge: Check your own GitHub repos. Search for 'api_key', 'sk-', 'OPENAI_API_KEY'. Did you find anything that shouldn't be public?

key_terms.reality: Maximum requests per minute/hour to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage
A billing unit: input and output tokens are counted and charged separately
Getting the response word by word instead of waiting for the full response

levels.title: Jupyter Notebooks
levels.tagline: Notebooks are the lab bench of AI engineering. You prototype here, then move what works into production.
objectives: Install and launch JupyterLab, Jupyter Notebook, or VS Code with the Jupyter extension
Use magic commands (%timeit, %%time, %matplotlib inline) to benchmark and visualize inline
Distinguish when to use notebooks vs scripts and apply the "explore in notebooks, ship in scripts" workflow
Identify and avoid common notebook traps: out-of-order execution, hidden state, and memory leaks
levels.problem:
Every AI paper, tutorial, and Kaggle competition uses Jupyter notebooks. They let you run code in pieces, see outputs inline, mix code with explanations, and iterate fast. If you try to learn AI without notebooks, you're doing math homework without scratch paper.

But notebooks have real traps. People use them for everything, including things they're terrible at. Knowing when to use a notebook and when to use a script will save you from debugging nightmares later.
levels.concept:
A notebook is a list of cells. Each cell is either code or text.

The kernel is a Python process running in the background. When you run a cell, it sends the code to the kernel, which executes it and sends back the result. All cells share the same kernel, so variables persist between cells.

code.code:
pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab

exercises: Open JupyterLab, create a notebook, and use %timeit to compare list comprehension vs numpy for creating an array of 100,000 random numbers
Create a notebook with both markdown and code cells that loads a CSV, displays a dataframe, and plots a chart. Then run Kernel > Restart & Run All to verify it works top to bottom
Take the code from code/notebook_tips.py, paste it into a Colab notebook, and run it with a free GPU

key_terms.reality: A separate Python process that executes cells and keeps variables in memory
An independently runnable unit in a notebook, either code or markdown
Special commands prefixed with % or %% that control the notebook environment
A JSON file containing cells, outputs, and metadata. Stands for IPython Notebook

An interactive document that mixes code, text, and visualizations in one place. You write code in cells, run them one at a time, and see results immediately — ideal for exploration, data analysis, and prototyping.
key_terms.myth: Jupyter is only for beginners — real engineers use .py files.
key_terms.analogy: A lab notebook for code. Scientists don't write their final paper directly — they experiment in a lab notebook first, then formalize. Jupyter is your AI lab notebook: try things, see results, iterate fast.
key_terms.example: Loading a dataset → viewing the first 10 rows → plotting a histogram → training a quick model → seeing that the learning rate is wrong — all in one document, with outputs visible. In a .py script, you'd have to re-run the whole file each time.
key_terms.why_matters: Jupyter is the lingua franca of AI research. Every major paper publishes notebooks. Every tutorial uses them. Every data scientist lives in them. Knowing when to use notebooks vs .py files is a core skill.
key_terms.common_trap: Using notebooks for production code. Notebooks are for exploration. Once you've found the right approach, extract the logic into .py modules with tests. Notebooks running in production are fragile and hard to debug.
key_terms.when_to_use: Data exploration, prototyping, visualization, tutorials, and research. Not for production serving or reusable libraries.

levels.title: Python Environments
levels.tagline: Dependency hell is real. Virtual environments are the cure.
objectives: Create isolated virtual environments using uv, venv, or conda
Write a pyproject.toml with optional dependency groups and generate lockfiles for reproducibility
Diagnose and fix common pitfalls: global installs, pip/conda mixing, CUDA version mismatches
Implement a per-phase environment strategy for projects with conflicting dependencies
levels.problem:
You install PyTorch 2.4 for a fine-tuning project. Next week, a different project needs PyTorch 2.1 because its CUDA build is pinned. You upgrade globally, and the first project breaks. You downgrade, and the second one breaks.

This is dependency hell. It happens constantly in AI/ML work because:

code.code:
# Create an isolated environment and install a package
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install numpy pandas

fill_in.prompt: You need to create a new Python environment and install packages. What's the missing line?
fill_in.before:
# Set up a new project
mkdir my-ai-project && cd my-ai-project
fill_in.after:
# Now install what you need
uv pip install torch numpy matplotlib
# Verify it worked
python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__)'
options: uv venv
pip install virtualenv
python -m venv .
conda create -n myproject python=3.13
fill_in.explain: `uv venv` creates a virtual environment in the current directory. It's 10-100x faster than `python -m venv` or `virtualenv`. After creating it, activate with `source .venv/bin/activate` and then install packages — they'll be isolated to this project only.

exercises: Run env_setup.sh and verify all checks pass
Create a second virtual environment, install a different version of numpy in it, and confirm the two environments are isolated
Write a pyproject.toml for a project that needs both PyTorch and the Anthropic SDK
Deliberately install a package globally (without activating a venv), notice where it goes, then uninstall it

key_terms.reality: An isolated directory containing a Python interpreter and packages, separate from system Python. Each project gets its own. Changes in one environment never affect another.
key_terms.myth: One global Python with everything installed is simpler.
key_terms.analogy: Each project is a separate kitchen. You don't want your curry spices mixing into your cake batter. Virtual environments keep your projects from contaminating each other.
key_terms.example: Project A: `uv venv && uv pip install torch==2.4.0`. Project B: `uv venv && uv pip install torch==2.1.0`. Both work. Zero conflicts. Try that globally and one overwrites the other.
key_terms.why_matters: This is the single most important Python skill for AI work. Every tutorial, repo, and job assumes you know venvs. Without them, you'll spend more time fixing environments than writing models.
key_terms.common_trap: Forgetting to activate the venv before installing. Your terminal prompt should show `(.venv)`. If it doesn't, you're about to install globally.
key_terms.scenario: You activate a venv but `pip list` still shows system packages. What's wrong?
key_terms.when_to_use: Before installing ANY packages for a new project. Always.
key_terms.mini_challenge: Create a venv, activate it, install numpy, deactivate, activate again, and verify numpy is still there.

key_terms.reality: A file listing every package and its exact version, guaranteeing identical installs across machines. `uv.lock`, `requirements.lock`, `poetry.lock` — different tools, same idea.
key_terms.myth: requirements.txt with >= versions is good enough.
key_terms.analogy: A lockfile is like a recipe that says '375g flour, brand King Arthur, protein 11.7%' instead of 'some flour.' Both make bread, but only one makes the SAME bread every time.
key_terms.example: You train a model with transformers==4.44.0. Your teammate installs from your lockfile and gets transformers==4.44.0 — not 4.45.0 which changed a default parameter and silently produces different results.
key_terms.why_matters: Without lockfiles, 'works on my machine' is inevitable. With lockfiles, everyone runs the exact same versions. This is non-negotiable for reproducibility in AI research and production.
key_terms.common_trap: Committing requirements.txt with loose versions (>=) instead of an exact lockfile. Loose versions mean different installs on different days.
key_terms.scenario: Your model's accuracy dropped 3% after a teammate reinstalled dependencies. What's the first thing to check?
key_terms.when_to_use: Every time you add or update a dependency in a project that anyone else will run.

key_terms.reality: The standard Python project configuration file, replacing setup.py/setup.cfg/requirements.txt in one file. Defines project metadata, dependencies, build system, and tool configs.
key_terms.myth: setup.py is still the standard way to configure Python projects.
key_terms.analogy: A pyproject.toml is a passport for your project. One document that tells every tool (pip, uv, ruff, mypy, pytest) everything they need to know about your project.
key_terms.example:
```toml
[project]
name = 'my-agent'
requires-python = '>=3.12'
dependencies = ['torch>=2.4', 'transformers>=4.44']
```
key_terms.why_matters: Modern Python tools (uv, ruff, mypy) read config from pyproject.toml. Using it means one config file to rule them all — no more scattering settings across 5 different files.
key_terms.common_trap: Putting pip-specific options in pyproject.toml that uv doesn't understand. pyproject.toml is a standard — stick to standard fields.
key_terms.mini_challenge: Create a pyproject.toml for a dummy project with one dependency. Run `uv pip install -e .` and verify it works.

key_terms.reality: uv is a fast Python package manager (10-100x faster than pip). It handles virtual environments, Python version management, and dependency resolution in a single tool.
key_terms.myth: pip is fast enough — no need for uv.
key_terms.analogy: pip is a bicycle. uv is a motorcycle. Both get you there, but one gets you there before the other person finishes tying their shoes.
key_terms.example: `uv pip install torch` — resolves and installs PyTorch + numpy + all deps in ~2 seconds vs ~45 seconds with pip. Over 100 installs, that's the difference between grabbing coffee and waiting.
key_terms.why_matters: In AI work, you create new environments constantly. Slow package installs add up to hours of waiting per week. uv turns 'pip install' from a coffee break into a blink.
key_terms.common_trap: Using `pip install` out of habit even though uv is installed. `uv pip install` is the same syntax but 10-100x faster. Just use it.
key_terms.when_to_use: Every time you'd use pip. `uv pip install` is a drop-in replacement.

key_terms.reality: PyTorch builds are tied to specific CUDA toolkit versions. Installing PyTorch compiled for CUDA 11.8 on a system with CUDA 12.4 drivers causes 'CUDA error: no kernel image available' — GPU acceleration silently fails or crashes.
key_terms.myth: Any PyTorch version works with any CUDA version.
key_terms.analogy: Like trying to play a Blu-ray in a DVD player. The disk (PyTorch) was made for one format (CUDA version). If they don't match, nothing plays.
key_terms.example: `nvidia-smi` shows CUDA 12.4. You need `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124` — the cu124 means CUDA 12.4. Installing the default `pip install torch` might give you a CPU-only build or wrong CUDA version.
key_terms.why_matters: The most common silent failure in AI setup. Your code runs, but it's 50x slower because it fell back to CPU without telling you.
key_terms.common_trap: Installing PyTorch with `pip install torch` without checking CUDA version first. Always check `nvidia-smi` then install the matching build.
key_terms.scenario: `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns False, but `nvidia-smi` shows a GPU. What's the most likely cause?
key_terms.mini_challenge: Run `nvidia-smi`, note the CUDA version, then check your PyTorch CUDA version with `python -c 'import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)'`. Do they match?

labs.title: Rescue the Broken Project
labs.prompt: Project A needs PyTorch 2.4. Project B needs PyTorch 2.1. Both use different CUDA versions. Arrange the solution:

steps.label: Check each project's requirements (pyproject.toml or README)
Create venv for Project A: uv venv && uv pip install torch==2.4.0
Create venv for Project B: uv venv && uv pip install torch==2.1.0
Generate lockfiles: uv lock (or pip freeze > requirements.lock)
Commit lockfiles so the team gets identical installs

labs.success: Two isolated environments, zero conflicts. This is the pattern for every AI project.

labs.title: Pick the Right Tool
labs.prompt: For each scenario, pick whether you'd reach for a venv, a lockfile, or pyproject.toml:

blocks.label: 'It worked yesterday but not today' — use a lockfile
'I need to share my project with 5 teammates' — use pyproject.toml + lockfile
'pip install everything globally, it's simpler' — NO, use a venv
'I need different torch versions for two projects' — use separate venvs

def bayes(prior, likelihood, false_positive_rate):
    evidence = likelihood * prior + false_positive_rate * (1 - prior)
    posterior = likelihood * prior / evidence
    return posterior

levels.title: Optimization
levels.tagline: Training a neural network is nothing more than finding the bottom of a valley.
objectives: Implement vanilla gradient descent, SGD with momentum, and Adam from scratch
Compare optimizer convergence on the Rosenbrock function and explain why Adam adapts per-weight learning rates
Distinguish convex from non-convex loss landscapes and explain the role of saddle points in high dimensions
Configure learning rate schedules (step decay, cosine annealing, warmup) for training stability
levels.problem:
You have a loss function. It tells you how wrong your model is. You have gradients. They tell you which direction makes the loss worse. Now you need a strategy for walking downhill.

The naive approach is simple: move opposite the gradient. Scale the step by some number called the learning rate. Repeat. This is gradient descent, and it works. But "works" has caveats. Too large a learning rate and you overshoot the valley entirely, bouncing between walls. Too small and you crawl toward the answer over thousands of unnecessary steps. Hit a saddle point and you stop moving even though you have not found a minimum.
levels.concept:
Optimization is finding the input values that minimize (or maximize) a function. In machine learning, the function is the loss. The inputs are the model's weights. Training is optimization.

The simplest optimizer. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Move each weight in the opposite direction of its gradient. Scale the step by the learning rate.
exercises: Learning rate sweep. Run vanilla gradient descent on the Rosenbrock function with learning rates [0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01]. Plot or print the final loss after 5000 steps for each. Find the largest learning rate that still converges.
Momentum comparison. Run SGD with momentum values [0.0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99] on the Rosenbrock function. Track the loss at every step. Which momentum value converges fastest? Which overshoots?

Saddle point escape. Define the function f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 (a saddle point at the origin). Start at (0.01, 0.01). Compare how vanilla GD, SGD with momentum, and Adam behave. Which escapes the saddle point?
Implement learning rate decay. Add an exponential decay schedule to the GradientDescent class: lr = lr_0 * 0.999^step. Compare convergence with and without decay on the Rosenbrock function.

key_terms.reality: Update weights by subtracting the gradient scaled by the learning rate. The most basic optimizer.
A scalar that controls how far each update moves the weights. Too large causes divergence. Too small wastes compute.
Accumulate past gradients into a velocity vector. Dampens oscillations and accelerates movement through consistent directions.
Stochastic gradient descent. Compute gradient on a random subset instead of the full dataset. Almost always means mini-batch SGD in practice.
A small subset of training data (32-256 samples) used to estimate the gradient. Balances speed and gradient accuracy.
Adaptive Moment Estimation. Tracks per-weight running averages of gradients and squared gradients to give each weight its own learning rate.
Adam's first and second moments are initialized to zero. Bias correction divides by (1 - beta^t) to compensate during early steps.
A function that adjusts the learning rate during training. Large steps early, small steps late.
A function where any local minimum is the global minimum. Gradient descent always finds it. Neural network losses are not convex.
A point where the gradient is zero but it is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others. Common in high dimensions.
The loss function plotted over weight space. Visualized by slicing along two random directions.
The optimizer has reached a point where further steps do not meaningfully reduce the loss.

levels.title: Information Theory
levels.tagline: Information theory measures surprise. Loss functions are built on it.

levels.problem:
You call `CrossEntropyLoss()` in every classification model you train. You see "perplexity" in every language model paper. You read about KL divergence in VAEs, distillation, and RLHF. These are not disconnected concepts. They are all the same idea wearing different hats.

Information theory gives you the language to reason about uncertainty, compression, and prediction. Claude Shannon invented it in 1948 to solve communication problems. Turns out, training a neural network is a communication problem: the model is trying to transmit the correct label through a noisy channel of learned weights.
levels.concept:
When something unlikely happens, it carries more information. A coin landing heads? Not surprising. A lottery win? Very surprising.

The information content of an event with probability p is:

The average surprise across all outcomes of a distribution. Measures irreducible uncertainty.

key_terms.reality: Reduction in uncertainty about X from knowing Y. Zero means independent.
Exponentiate and normalize. Maps any real-valued vector to a valid probability distribution.
Exponential of cross-entropy. The effective vocabulary size the model is choosing from at each step.

levels.title: Dimensionality Reduction
levels.tagline: High-dimensional data has structure. You find it by looking from the right angle.
levels.prerequisites: Phase 1, Lessons 01 (Linear Algebra Intuition), 02 (Vectors, Matrices & Operations), 03 (Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors), 06 (Probability & Distributions)
objectives: Implement PCA from scratch: center data, compute the covariance matrix, eigendecompose, and project

levels.problem:
You have a dataset with 784 features per sample. Maybe it is pixel values of handwritten digits. Maybe it is gene expression levels. Maybe it is user behavior signals. You cannot visualize 784 dimensions. You cannot plot them. You cannot even think about them.

But most of those 784 features are redundant. The actual information lives on a much smaller surface. A handwritten "7" does not need 784 independent numbers to describe it. It needs a few: the angle of the stroke, the length of the crossbar, how much it leans. The rest is noise.
levels.concept:
High-dimensional spaces are unintuitive. Three things break as dimensions grow.

**Distance becomes meaningless.** In high dimensions, the distance between any two random points converges to the same value. If every point is roughly the same distance from every other point, nearest-neighbor search stops working.

code.code:
import numpy as np

class PCA:
    def __init__(self, n_components):
        self.n_components = n_components
        self.components = None
        self.mean = None
        self.eigenvalues = None
        self.explained_variance_ratio_ = None

    def fit(self, X):
        self.mean = np.mean(X, axis=0)
        X_centered = X - self.mean

        cov_matrix = np.cov(X_centered, rowvar=False)

        eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov_matrix)

        sorted_idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1]
        eigenvalues = eigenvalues[sorted_idx]
        eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, sorted_idx]

        self.components = eigenvectors[:, :self.n_components].T
        self.eigenvalues = eigenvalues[:self.n_components]
        total_var = np.sum(eigenvalues)
        self.explained_variance_ratio_ = self.eigenvalues / total_var
# ...

exercises: Modify the PCA class to support inverse_transform. Reconstruct MNIST digits from 10, 50, and 200 components. Print the reconstruction error (mean squared difference from the original) for each.

key_terms.reality: Distances, volumes, and data density all behave counterintuitively as dimensions grow. Models need exponentially more data to compensate.
Rotate your coordinate system so the axes align with the directions of maximum variance, then drop the low-variance axes.
An eigenvector of the covariance matrix. The direction in feature space along which the data varies most.

key_terms.reality: The fraction of total variance captured by one principal component. Sum the top k ratios to see how much k components preserve.
A symmetric matrix where entry (i,j) measures how feature i and feature j move together. Diagonal entries are individual variances.
A nonlinear method that maps high-dimensional data to 2D by preserving pairwise neighborhood probabilities. Good for visualization, not for preprocessing.
A nonlinear method based on topological data analysis. Preserves both local and some global structure. Scales better than t-SNE.
Controls the effective number of neighbors each point considers. Low perplexity focuses on very local structure. High perplexity captures broader patterns.

key_terms.myth: The surface the data lives on
key_terms.reality: A lower-dimensional surface embedded in a higher-dimensional space. A sheet of paper crumpled in 3D is a 2D manifold.

Given any matrix A, SVD factors it into:

- Sigma scales along each axis (stretches or compresses)

levels.title: Tensor Operations
levels.tagline: Tensors are the common language between data and deep learning. Every image, every sentence, every gradient flows through them.
levels.prerequisites: Phase 1, Lessons 01 (Linear Algebra Intuition), 02 (Vectors, Matrices & Operations)
objectives: Implement a tensor class with shape, strides, reshape, transpose, and element-wise operations from scratch
Apply broadcasting rules to operate on tensors of different shapes without copying data
Write einsum expressions for dot products, matrix multiplications, outer products, and batched operations
Trace the exact tensor shapes through every step of multi-head attention
levels.problem:
You build a transformer. The forward pass looks clean. You run it and get: `RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x768 and 512x768)`. You stare at the shapes. You try a transpose. Now it says `Expected 4D input (got 3D input)`. You add an unsqueeze. Something else breaks.

Shape errors are the most common bug in deep learning code. They are not hard conceptually -- each operation has a shape contract -- but they multiply fast. A transformer has dozens of reshapes, transposes, and broadcasts chained together. One wrong axis and the error cascades. Worse, some shape mistakes do not throw errors at all. They silently produce garbage by broadcasting along the wrong dimension or summing over the wrong axis.
levels.concept:
A tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers with a uniform data type. The number of dimensions is the **rank** (or **order**). Each dimension is an **axis**. The **shape** is a tuple listing the size along each axis.

Total elements = product of all sizes. A shape `(2, 3, 4)` holds `2 * 3 * 4 = 24` elements.
exercises: Easy -- Reshape round-trip. Take a tensor of shape (2, 3, 4). Reshape it to (6, 4), then to (24,), then back to (2, 3, 4). Verify element order is preserved at each step by printing the flat data.

Medium -- Implement broadcasting. Extend the Tensor class with a broadcast_to(shape) method that expands dimensions of size 1 to match a target shape. Then modify _elementwise_op to automatically broadcast before operating. Test with shapes (3, 1) and (1, 4) producing (3, 4).

Hard -- Build einsum from scratch. Implement a basic einsum(subscripts, *tensors) function that handles at least: dot product (i,i->), matrix multiply (ij,jk->ik), outer product (i,j->ij), and transpose (ij->ji). Parse the subscript string, identify contracted indices, and loop over all index combinations. Compare your results against np.einsum.

Hard -- Attention shape tracker. Write a function that takes batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim, and num_heads as inputs and prints the exact shape at every step of multi-head attention: input, Q/K/V projection, head split, attention scores, softmax weights, weighted sum, head merge, output projection. Verify against the demo_attention_einsum() output.

key_terms.reality: A multi-dimensional array with uniform type and defined shape, strides, and operations
The number of axes. A matrix has rank 2, not rank equal to its matrix rank
A tuple listing the size along each axis. (2, 3) means 2 rows, 3 columns
The number of elements to skip to advance one position along each axis

key_terms.myth: It just works when shapes differ
key_terms.reality: A strict set of rules: align from right, dimensions must be equal or one must be 1
Elements stored sequentially in memory with no gaps or reordering from the logical layout

key_terms.reality: A general notation that expresses any tensor contraction, outer product, trace, or transpose in one line

levels.title: Numerical Stability
levels.tagline: Floating point is a leaky abstraction. It will bite you during training, and you will not see it coming.
objectives: Implement numerically stable softmax and log-sum-exp using the max-subtraction trick
Identify overflow, underflow, and catastrophic cancellation in floating-point computations
Verify analytical gradients against numerical gradients using centered finite differences
Explain why bfloat16 is preferred over float16 for training and how loss scaling prevents gradient underflow
levels.problem:
Your model trains for three hours, then the loss becomes NaN. You add a print statement. The logits are fine at step 9,000. At step 9,001 they are `inf`. By step 9,002 every gradient is `nan` and training is dead.

Or: your model trains to completion but accuracy is 2% worse than the paper claims. You check everything. Architecture matches. Hyperparameters match. Data matches. The problem is that the paper used float32 and you used float16 without the right scaling. Thirty-two bits of accumulated rounding error quietly ate your accuracy.
levels.concept:
Computers store real numbers as floating point values following the IEEE 754 standard. A float has three parts: a sign bit, an exponent, and a mantissa (significand).

The mantissa determines precision (how many significant digits). The exponent determines range (how large or small a number can be).
exercises: Catastrophic cancellation. Compute the variance of [1000000.0, 1000001.0, 1000002.0] using the naive formula E[x^2] - E[x]^2 in float32. Then compute it using Welford's online algorithm. Compare the errors against the true variance (0.6667).
Precision hunt. Find the smallest positive float32 value x such that 1.0 + x == 1.0 in Python. This is the machine epsilon. Verify it matches numpy.finfo(numpy.float32).eps.

Log-sum-exp edge cases. Test your logsumexp_stable function with: (a) all values equal, (b) one value much larger than the rest, (c) all values very negative (-1000). Verify it gives correct results where the naive version fails.

key_terms.reality: International standard defining binary floating point formats, rounding rules, and special values (inf, nan). Every modern CPU and GPU implements it.
The smallest value e such that 1.0 + e != 1.0 in a given float format. For float32, it is about 1.19e-7.
When subtracting nearly equal floating point numbers, significant digits cancel and rounding noise dominates the result.
A result exceeds the maximum representable value and becomes inf. exp(89) overflows float32.
A result is closer to zero than the smallest representable positive number and becomes 0.0. exp(-104) underflows float32.
Computing log(sum(exp(x))) by factoring out exp(max(x)) to prevent overflow and underflow. Used in softmax, cross-entropy, and log-probability math.
Subtracting max(logits) before exponentiating. Numerically identical result, no overflow possible.
Comparing analytical gradients from backpropagation against numerical gradients from finite differences to catch implementation bugs.
Using lower-precision floats for speed-critical operations and higher-precision floats for numerically sensitive operations. Typical speedup is 2-3x.
Multiplying the loss by a large constant before backprop so gradients stay in float16's representable range, then dividing by the same constant before weight updates.
Google's 16-bit format with 8 exponent bits (same range as float32) and 7 mantissa bits (less precision than float16). Preferred for training.
Scaling the gradient vector so its norm does not exceed a threshold. Prevents exploding gradients from ruining weights.
Special float value from undefined operations (0/0, inf-inf, sqrt(-1)). Propagates through all subsequent arithmetic.
Special float value from overflow or division by zero. Can combine to produce NaN (inf - inf, inf * 0).
Approximating a derivative by evaluating f(x+h) and f(x-h) and dividing by 2h. Slow but reliable for verification.

levels.title: Norms and Distances
levels.tagline: Your distance function defines what "similar" means. Choose wrong and everything downstream breaks.
levels.prerequisites: Phase 1, Lessons 01 (Linear Algebra Intuition), 02 (Vectors, Matrices & Operations)
objectives: Implement L1, L2, cosine, Mahalanobis, Jaccard, and edit distance functions from scratch

levels.problem:
You have two vectors. Maybe they are word embeddings. Maybe they are user profiles. Maybe they are pixel arrays. You need to know: how close are they?

The answer depends entirely on which distance function you pick. Two data points can be nearest neighbors under one metric and far apart under another. Your KNN classifier, your recommendation engine, your vector database, your clustering algorithm, your loss function -- they all depend on this choice. Get it wrong and your model optimizes for the wrong thing.
levels.concept:
A norm measures the "size" of a vector. Every distance function between two vectors can be written as the norm of their difference: d(a, b) = ||a - b||. So understanding norms is understanding distances.

The L1 norm sums the absolute values of all components.

Implement a function that takes a dataset and a query point and returns the nearest neighbor under L1, L2, cosine, and Mahalanobis distance. Find a dataset where all four disagree on which point is nearest.

Sum of absolute component values. Produces sparsity in optimization. Robust to outliers
Square root of sum of squared components. The straight-line distance in Euclidean space
The p-th root of the sum of p-th powers of absolute components. L1 and L2 are special cases
The maximum absolute component value. The limit of Lp as p approaches infinity
Dot product normalized by both magnitudes. Ranges from -1 to +1. Ignores vector length
Converts cosine similarity to a distance. Ranges from 0 to 2
Sum of component-wise products. Equals cosine similarity times both magnitudes
L2 distance in a space that has been whitened (decorrelated and normalized) using the data covariance matrix
Size of intersection divided by size of union. For sets, not vectors
Minimum insertions, deletions, and substitutions to transform one string into another
Not a true distance (not symmetric). Measures extra bits from using Q to encode P
Minimum work to transport mass from one distribution to another. A true metric
Algorithms (HNSW, LSH, IVF) that find approximately closest points much faster than exact search
Hierarchical Navigable Small World graph. Multi-layer graph for fast approximate nearest neighbor search
Adding the L1 norm of weights to the loss. Drives weights to zero (sparsity)
Adding the squared L2 norm of weights to the loss. Shrinks weights toward zero without sparsity
Combines L1 and L2 regularization. Handles correlated feature groups better than either alone

levels.title: Statistics for Machine Learning
levels.tagline: Statistics is how you know if your model actually works or just got lucky.
objectives: Compute descriptive statistics, Pearson/Spearman correlation, and covariance matrices from scratch
Perform hypothesis tests (t-test, chi-squared) and interpret p-values and confidence intervals correctly
Use bootstrap resampling to construct confidence intervals for any metric without distributional assumptions

levels.problem:
You trained two models. Model A scores 0.87 on your test set. Model B scores 0.89. You deploy Model B. Three weeks later, production metrics are worse than before. What happened?

Model B did not actually outperform Model A. The 0.02 difference was noise. Your test set was too small, or the variance too high, or both. You shipped randomness dressed up as improvement.
levels.concept:
Before you model anything, you need to know what your data looks like. Descriptive statistics compress a dataset into a few numbers that capture its shape.

**Measures of central tendency** answer "where is the middle?"

levels.title: Sampling Methods
levels.tagline: Sampling is how AI explores the space of possibilities.
objectives: Implement inverse CDF, rejection, and importance sampling from scratch using only uniform random numbers

levels.problem:
A language model finishes processing your prompt and produces a vector of 50,000 logits. One for every token in its vocabulary. Now it has to pick one. How?

If it always picks the highest-probability token, every response is identical. Deterministic. Boring. If it picks uniformly at random, the output is gibberish. The answer lives somewhere between these extremes, and that somewhere is controlled by sampling.
levels.concept:
Sampling appears in four fundamental roles across AI and machine learning:

**Generation.** Language models, diffusion models, and GANs all produce output by sampling. The sampling algorithm directly controls creativity, coherence, and diversity. Temperature, top-k, and nucleus sampling are the knobs that engineers turn daily.
exercises: Implement inverse CDF sampling for the Cauchy distribution. The CDF is F(x) = 0.5 + arctan(x)/pi. Generate 10,000 samples and plot the histogram against the true PDF. Notice the heavy tails (extreme values far from center).

Estimate the integral of sin(x) from 0 to pi using Monte Carlo with 1,000, 10,000, and 100,000 samples. Compare the error at each level. Verify that the error scales as O(1/sqrt(N)).

Implement Metropolis-Hastings to sample from a 2D distribution p(x, y) proportional to exp(-(x^2  y^2 + x^2 + y^2 - 8x - 8*y) / 2). Plot the samples and the chain trajectory. Experiment with different proposal standard deviations.

Every time you train a linear regression, you solve a linear system. Every time you compute a least-squares fit, you solve a linear system. The equation Ax = b appears everywhere. A is a matrix of known coefficients. b is a vector of known outputs. x is the vector of unknowns you want to find. objectives: Test whether a function is convex using the definition, second derivative, and Hessian criteria

levels.problem:
Lesson 08 taught you gradient descent, momentum, and Adam. Those optimizers walk downhill on any surface. But they come with no guarantees. Gradient descent on a non-convex landscape might land in a bad local minimum, get stuck on a saddle point, or oscillate forever. You used it anyway because neural networks are non-convex and there is no alternative.

But many problems in machine learning are convex. Linear regression, logistic regression, SVMs, LASSO, ridge regression. For these, something stronger exists: optimization with mathematical guarantees. A convex problem has exactly one valley. Any algorithm that walks downhill will reach the global minimum. No restarts needed. No learning rate schedules. No prayer.
levels.concept:
A set S is convex if for any two points in S, the line segment between them also lies entirely in S.

Formal test: for any points x, y in S and any t in [0, 1], the point tx + (1-t)y is also in S.

code.code:
import random
import math

def check_convexity(f, dim, bounds=(-5, 5), samples=1000):
    violations = 0
    for _ in range(samples):
        x = [random.uniform(*bounds) for _ in range(dim)]
        y = [random.uniform(*bounds) for _ in range(dim)]
        t = random.uniform(0, 1)
        mid = [t * xi + (1 - t) * yi for xi, yi in zip(x, y)]
        lhs = f(mid)
        rhs = t * f(x) + (1 - t) * f(y)
        if lhs > rhs + 1e-10:
            violations += 1
    return violations == 0, violations

import math

class Complex:
    ...

def dft(x):
    N = len(x)
    result = []
    for k in range(N):
        total = Complex(0, 0)
        for n in range(N):
            angle = -2 * math.pi * k * n / N
            w = Complex(math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle))
            xn = x[n] if isinstance(x[n], Complex) else Complex(x[n])
            total = total + xn * w
        result.append(total)
    return result

levels.problem:
Many AI systems involve randomness that evolves over time. Not static randomness -- structured, sequential randomness where each step depends on what came before.

Language models generate tokens one at a time. Each token depends on the previous context. The model outputs a probability distribution, samples from it, and moves on. That is a stochastic process.
levels.concept:
Start at position 0. At each step, flip a fair coin. Heads: move right (+1). Tails: move left (-1).

After n steps, your position is the sum of n random +/-1 values. The expected position is 0 (the walk is unbiased). But the expected distance from the origin grows as sqrt(n).

code.code:
import numpy as np

def random_walk_1d(n_steps, seed=None):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    steps = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=n_steps)
    positions = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(steps)])
    return positions


def random_walk_2d(n_steps, seed=None):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    directions = rng.choice(4, size=n_steps)
    dx = np.zeros(n_steps)
    dy = np.zeros(n_steps)
    dx[directions == 0] = 1   # right
    dx[directions == 1] = -1  # left
    dy[directions == 2] = 1   # up
    dy[directions == 3] = -1  # down
    x = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(dx)])
    y = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(dy)])
    return x, y

exercises: Simulate 1000 random walks of 10000 steps. Plot the distribution of final positions. Verify it is approximately Gaussian with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(10000) = 100.

Why? Trees handle mixed feature types (numeric and categorical) without preprocessing. They handle nonlinear relationships without feature engineering. They are interpretable: you can look at the tree and see exactly why a prediction was made. And random forests, which average many trees, are highly resistant to overfitting on moderate-sized datasets.
levels.concept:
A decision tree partitions the feature space into rectangular regions by asking a sequence of yes/no questions.

Each internal node tests a feature against a threshold. Each leaf node makes a prediction. To classify a new data point, you start at the root and follow the branches until you reach a leaf.

levels.problem:
You have two classes of data points and need to draw a line (or hyperplane) separating them. Infinitely many lines could work. Which one should you pick?

The one with the biggest margin. The margin is the distance between the decision boundary and the nearest data points on each side. A wider margin means the classifier is more confident and generalizes better to unseen data.
levels.concept:
Given linearly separable data with labels y_i in {-1, +1} and feature vectors x_i, we want a hyperplane w^T x + b = 0 that separates the classes.

The distance from a point x_i to the hyperplane is:

code.code:
def hinge_loss(X, y, w, b):
    n = len(X)
    total_loss = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        margin = y[i] * (dot(w, X[i]) + b)
        total_loss += max(0.0, 1.0 - margin)
    return total_loss / n

levels.problem:
You have a dataset. A new data point arrives. You need to classify it or predict its value. Instead of learning parameters from the data (like linear regression or SVMs), you just find the K training points closest to the new point and let them vote.

This is K-nearest neighbors. There is no training phase. No parameters to learn. No loss function to minimize. You store the entire training set and compute distances at prediction time.
levels.concept:
Given a dataset of labeled points and a new query point:

1. Compute the distance from the query to every point in the dataset
2. Sort by distance
3. Take the K closest points
4. For classification: majority vote among the K neighbors
5. For regression: average (or weighted average) of the K neighbors' values

levels.problem:
Every ML lesson so far has assumed labeled data: "here is an input, here is the correct output." In the real world, labels are expensive. A hospital has millions of patient records but no one has manually tagged each one with a disease category. An e-commerce site has millions of user sessions but no one has hand-labeled customer segments. A security team has network logs but nobody has flagged every anomaly.

Unsupervised learning finds patterns without being told what to look for. It groups similar data points, discovers hidden structures, and surfaces anomalies. If supervised learning is learning from a textbook with an answer key, unsupervised learning is staring at raw data until the patterns reveal themselves.
levels.concept:
Clustering assigns each data point to a group (cluster) so that points within the same group are more similar to each other than to points in other groups. The question is always: what does "similar" mean?

K-Means partitions data into exactly K clusters. Each cluster has a centroid (its center of mass), and every point belongs to the nearest centroid.

levels.concept:

**Scaling:** Put features on the same range so distance-based algorithms (K-Means, KNN, SVM) treat all features equally. Min-max scaling maps to [0, 1]. Standardization (z-score) maps to mean=0, std=1.

levels.title: Model Evaluation
levels.tagline: A model is only as good as the way you measure it.

levels.problem:
You trained a model. It gets 95% accuracy on your data. Is it good?

Maybe. Maybe not. If 95% of your data belongs to one class, a model that always predicts that class gets 95% accuracy while being completely useless. If you evaluated on the same data you trained on, the 95% number is meaningless because the model just memorized the answers. If your dataset has a time component and you randomly shuffled before splitting, your model might be using future data to predict the past.
levels.concept:
Three splits, three purposes:

- **Training set**: the model learns from this data. It sees these examples during training.
- **Validation set**: used to tune hyperparameters and select between models. The model never trains on this data, but your decisions are influenced by it.
- **Test set**: touched exactly once, at the very end, to report final performance. If you look at test performance and then go back to change your model, it is no longer a test set. It has become a second validation set.

code.code:
import random
import math


def train_val_test_split(X, y, train_ratio=0.6, val_ratio=0.2, seed=42):
    random.seed(seed)
    n = len(X)
    indices = list(range(n))
    random.shuffle(indices)

    train_end = int(n * train_ratio)
    val_end = int(n * (train_ratio + val_ratio))

    train_idx = indices[:train_end]
    val_idx = indices[train_end:val_end]
    test_idx = indices[val_end:]

    X_train = [X[i] for i in train_idx]
    y_train = [y[i] for i in train_idx]
    X_val = [X[i] for i in val_idx]
    y_val = [y[i] for i in val_idx]
    X_test = [X[i] for i in test_idx]
    y_test = [y[i] for i in test_idx]

    return X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test

levels.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
levels.tagline: Every model error comes from one of three sources: bias, variance, or noise. You can only control the first two.
levels.prerequisites: Phase 2, Lessons 01-09 (ML basics, regression, classification, evaluation)
objectives: Derive the bias-variance decomposition of expected prediction error and explain the role of irreducible noise
Diagnose whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance using training and test error patterns

levels.problem:
You trained a model. It has some error on test data. Where does that error come from?

If your model is too simple (linear regression on a curved dataset), it will consistently miss the true pattern. That is bias. If your model is too complex (degree-20 polynomial on 15 data points), it will fit the training data perfectly but give wildly different predictions on new data. That is variance.
levels.concept:
Bias measures how far off your model's average prediction is from the true value. If you trained the same model on many different training sets drawn from the same distribution and averaged the predictions, bias is the gap between that average and the truth.

High bias means the model is too rigid to capture the real pattern. A straight line fit to a parabola will always miss the curve, no matter how much data you give it. This is underfitting.

code.code:
def true_function(x):
    return np.sin(1.5 * x) + 0.5 * x

def generate_data(n_samples=30, noise_std=0.5, x_range=(-3, 3), seed=None):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    x = rng.uniform(x_range[0], x_range[1], n_samples)
    y = true_function(x) + rng.normal(0, noise_std, n_samples)
    return x, y

Increase the training set size from 30 to 300. How does this affect the variance component? Does the optimal polynomial degree shift?

key_terms.reality: Systematic error from wrong assumptions. The gap between the average model prediction and truth.
Error from sensitivity to training data. How much predictions change across different training sets.
Error from randomness in the true data-generating process. No model can eliminate it.
Model has high bias. It misses the real pattern even on training data.
Model has high variance. It fits noise in training data that does not generalize.
Adding a penalty to reduce model complexity, trading bias for lower variance.

The capacity of a model to fit arbitrary patterns. Controlled by architecture, features, or regularization.

levels.problem:
A single decision tree is fast to train and easy to interpret, but it overfits. A single linear model underfits on complex boundaries. You could spend days engineering the perfect model architecture. Or you could combine a bunch of imperfect models and get something better than any of them individually.

Ensemble methods do exactly this. They are the most reliable technique for winning Kaggle competitions on tabular data, they power most production ML systems, and they illustrate the bias-variance tradeoff in action. Bagging reduces variance. Boosting reduces bias. Stacking learns which models to trust on which inputs.

Suppose you have N independent classifiers, each with accuracy p > 0.5. The majority vote has accuracy:

For 21 classifiers each with 60% accuracy, majority vote accuracy is about 74%. With 101 classifiers, it rises to 84%. The errors cancel out when the models make different mistakes.

levels.tagline: Hyperparameters are the knobs you turn before training starts. Turning them well is the difference between a mediocre model and a great one.

levels.problem:
Your gradient boosting model has a learning rate, number of trees, max depth, min samples per leaf, subsample ratio, and column sample ratio. That is six hyperparameters. If each has 5 reasonable values, the grid has 5^6 = 15,625 combinations. Training each takes 10 seconds. That is 43 hours of compute to try them all.

Grid search is the obvious approach and the worst one at scale. Random search does better with less compute. Bayesian optimization does even better by learning from past evaluations. Knowing which strategy to use, and which hyperparameters actually matter, saves days of wasted GPU time.
levels.concept:
Parameters are learned during training (weights, biases, split thresholds). Hyperparameters are set before training starts and control how learning happens.

Grid search evaluates every combination of specified values. It is exhaustive and easy to understand, but scales exponentially with the number of hyperparameters.

code.code:
def grid_search(model_fn, param_grid, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val):
    keys = list(param_grid.keys())
    values = list(param_grid.values())
    best_score = -float("inf")
    best_params = None
    n_evals = 0

    for combo in itertools.product(*values):
        params = dict(zip(keys, combo))
        model = model_fn(**params)
        model.fit(X_train, y_train)
        score = evaluate(model, X_val, y_val)
        n_evals += 1

        if score > best_score:
            best_score = score
            best_params = params

    return best_params, best_score, n_evals

A categorical column gained a new value in production that the encoder has never seen.
levels.concept:
A pipeline is an ordered sequence of data transformations followed by a model. Each step takes the output of the previous step as input. The entire pipeline is fitted once on training data. At inference time, the same fitted pipeline transforms new data and produces predictions.

The pipeline guarantees:
- Transformations are fitted only on training data (no leakage)
- The same transformations are applied at inference time
- The entire object can be serialized and deployed as one artifact

levels.title: Naive Bayes
levels.tagline: The "naive" assumption is wrong, and it works anyway. That's the beauty of it.
objectives: Implement Multinomial Naive Bayes from scratch with Laplace smoothing for text classification
Explain why the naive independence assumption is mathematically wrong but produces correct class rankings in practice

levels.problem:
You need to classify text. Emails into spam or not-spam. Customer reviews into positive or negative. Support tickets into categories. You have thousands of features (one per word) and limited training data.

Most classifiers choke here. Logistic regression needs enough samples to estimate thousands of weights reliably. Decision trees split on one word at a time and overfit wildly. KNN in 10,000 dimensions is meaningless because every point is equally far from every other point.
levels.concept:
Bayes' theorem flips conditional probabilities:

We want `P(class | features)` -- the probability that a document belongs to a class given the words in it. We can compute this from:
- `P(features | class)` -- the likelihood of seeing these words in documents of this class
- `P(class)` -- the prior probability of the class (how common is spam in general?)
- `P(features)` -- the evidence, same for all classes, so we can ignore it when comparing

code.code:
class MultinomialNB:
    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0):
        self.alpha = alpha

    def fit(self, X, y):
        classes = np.unique(y)
        n_classes = len(classes)
        n_features = X.shape[1]

        self.classes_ = classes
        self.class_log_prior_ = np.zeros(n_classes)
        self.feature_log_prob_ = np.zeros((n_classes, n_features))

        for i, c in enumerate(classes):
            X_c = X[y == c]
            self.class_log_prior_[i] = np.log(X_c.shape[0] / X.shape[0])
            counts = X_c.sum(axis=0) + self.alpha
            self.feature_log_prob_[i] = np.log(counts / counts.sum())

        return self

exercises: Smoothing experiment. Train MultinomialNB on text data with alpha values of 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, and 100.0. Plot accuracy vs alpha. Where does performance peak? Why does very high alpha hurt?

levels.problem:
You have data ordered by time. Daily sales, hourly temperature, per-minute CPU usage, weekly stock prices. You want to predict the next value, the next week, the next quarter.

levels.concept:
Standard ML assumes i.i.d. -- independent and identically distributed. Each sample is drawn from the same distribution, independently of other samples. Time series violates both:

- **Not independent.** Today's stock price depends on yesterday's. This week's sales correlate with last week's.
- **Not identically distributed.** The distribution shifts over time. Sales in December look different from sales in March.

def make_lag_features(series, n_lags):
    n = len(series)
    X = np.full((n, n_lags), np.nan)
    for lag in range(1, n_lags + 1):
        X[lag:, lag - 1] = series[:-lag]
    valid = ~np.isnan(X).any(axis=1)
    return X[valid], series[valid]

levels.problem:
A credit card is used in New York at 2pm, then in Tokyo at 2:05pm. A factory sensor reads 150 degrees when the normal range is 80-120. A server sends 50,000 requests per second when the daily average is 200.

These are anomalies. Finding them matters. Fraud costs billions. Equipment failures cost downtime. Network intrusions cost data.
levels.concept:
Not all anomalies are the same:

- **Point anomalies.** A single data point that is unusual regardless of context. A temperature reading of 500 degrees. A transaction of $50,000 from an account that normally spends $50.
- **Contextual anomalies.** A data point that is unusual given its context. A temperature of 90 degrees is normal in summer, anomalous in winter. Same value, different context.
- **Collective anomalies.** A sequence of data points that is unusual as a group, even though each individual point might be normal. Five login failures is normal. Fifty in a row is a brute-force attack.

code.code:
def zscore_detect(X, threshold=3.0):
    mean = X.mean(axis=0)
    std = X.std(axis=0)
    std[std == 0] = 1.0
    z = np.abs((X - mean) / std)
    return z.max(axis=1) > threshold

import numpy as np


def make_imbalanced_data(n_majority=950, n_minority=50, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)

    X_maj = rng.randn(n_majority, 2) * 1.0 + np.array([0.0, 0.0])
    X_min = rng.randn(n_minority, 2) * 0.8 + np.array([2.5, 2.5])

    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n_majority), np.ones(n_minority)])

    shuffle_idx = rng.permutation(len(y))
    return X[shuffle_idx], y[shuffle_idx]

levels.problem:
You have 500 features. Your model trains slowly, overfits constantly, and nobody can explain what it learned. You add more features hoping to improve performance. It gets worse.

This is the curse of dimensionality in action. As the number of features grows, the volume of the feature space explodes. Data points become sparse. Distances between points converge. The model needs exponentially more data to find real patterns. Noise features drown out signal features. Overfitting becomes the default.
levels.concept:
Every feature selection method falls into one of three categories:

**Filter methods** score each feature independently using a statistical measure. They do not use a model. Fast, but they miss feature interactions.

import numpy as np


def make_feature_selection_data(n_samples=500, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)

    x1 = rng.randn(n_samples)
    x2 = rng.randn(n_samples)
    x3 = rng.randn(n_samples)
    x4 = x1 + 0.1 * rng.randn(n_samples)
    x5 = x2 + 0.1 * rng.randn(n_samples)

    informative = np.column_stack([x1, x2, x3, x4, x5])

    correlated = np.column_stack([
        x1 * 0.9 + 0.1 * rng.randn(n_samples),
        x2 * 0.8 + 0.2 * rng.randn(n_samples),
        x3 * 0.7 + 0.3 * rng.randn(n_samples),
        x1 * 0.5 + x2 * 0.5 + 0.1 * rng.randn(n_samples),
        x2 * 0.6 + x3 * 0.4 + 0.1 * rng.randn(n_samples),
    ])

    noise = rng.randn(n_samples, 10) * 0.5

    X = np.hstack([informative, correlated, noise])
    y = (2 * x1 - 1.5 * x2 + x3 + 0.5 * rng.randn(n_samples) > 0).astype(int)

levels.problem:
You know vectors and dot products. You know that a matrix transforms inputs into outputs. But how does a machine *learn* which transformation to use?

The perceptron answers this. It's the simplest possible learning machine: take some inputs, multiply by weights, add a bias, and make a binary decision. Then adjust. That's it. Every neural network ever built is layers of this idea stacked together.

The step function is brutal: if the weighted sum plus bias is >= 0, output 1. Otherwise, output 0.

In 1969, Minsky and Papert proved this limitation was fatal: a single-layer network cannot learn XOR. Not "struggles to learn" -- mathematically cannot. The XOR truth table places [0,1] and [1,0] on one side, [0,0] and [1,1] on the other. No single line separates them.

levels.title: Backpropagation from Scratch
levels.tagline: Backpropagation is the algorithm that makes learning possible. Without it, neural networks are just expensive random number generators.
objectives: Implement a Value-based autograd engine that builds a computational graph and computes gradients via topological sort

levels.problem:
Your network has a single hidden layer with 768 inputs and 3072 outputs. That's 2,359,296 weights. It made a wrong prediction. Which weights caused the error? Testing each weight individually means 2.3 million forward passes. Backpropagation computes all 2.3 million gradients in a single backward pass. That's not an optimization. That's the difference between trainable and impossible.

The naive approach: take one weight, nudge it by a tiny amount, run the forward pass again, measure whether the loss went up or down. That gives you the gradient for that weight. Now do it for every weight in the network. Multiply by thousands of training steps and millions of data points. You'd need geological time to train anything useful.
levels.concept:
You saw the chain rule in Phase 01, Lesson 05. Quick recap: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x). You multiply derivatives along the chain.

In a neural network, the "chain" is the sequence of operations from input to loss. Each layer applies weights, adds biases, passes through an activation. The loss function compares the final output to the target. Backpropagation traces this chain backward, computing how each operation contributed to the error.
exercises: Add a __sub__ method to the Value class (a - b = a + (-1 * b)). Then implement a __neg__ method. Verify that the gradients are correct by comparing with manual calculation for a simple expression like (a - b)^2.

levels.title: Loss Functions
levels.tagline: Your network makes a prediction. The ground truth says otherwise. How wrong is it? That number is the loss. Pick the wrong loss function and your model optimizes for the wrong thing entirely.

levels.problem:
A model minimizing MSE on a classification problem will confidently predict 0.5 for everything. It's minimizing loss. It's also useless.

The loss function is the only thing your model actually optimizes. Not accuracy. Not F1 score. Not whatever metric you report to your manager. The optimizer takes the gradient of the loss function and adjusts weights to make that number smaller. If the loss function doesn't capture what you care about, the model will find the mathematically cheapest way to satisfy it, and that way is almost never what you wanted.
levels.concept:
The default for regression. Compute the squared difference between prediction and target, average over all samples.

Why squaring matters: it penalizes large errors quadratically. An error of 2 costs 4x as much as an error of 1. An error of 10 costs 100x. This makes MSE sensitive to outliers -- a single wildly wrong prediction dominates the loss.
